title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
purpose: It establishes 'Ali's walaya and the Imams' exclusive knowledge by citing Ismaili authorities' Qur'anic exegesis and then narrating cases in which 'Ali and al-Hasan answer questions that others could not.

points.text: The author cites Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman's Book of the Foster-Suckling, which reads 'the righteous of the believers' in Q 66:4 as designating 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and woman.

On the same authority, Qur'anic uses of 'righteous' — 'their father was righteous' and 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' — are interpreted as referring to an Imam and to the Imams among God's servants.

The Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, in a Friday sermon, likened himself in the physical world to the Pen in the spiritual world, setting four ranks beneath it, each preceded by a spiritual rank guiding it upward, so that the foundation faces the tablet and engraves upon it what it derives from the spiritual world.

In an account from Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, a messenger of the king of Rum brings money to Medina to test the Prophet's successor with three questions: what is not God's, what is not with God, and what God does not know.
Abu Bakr and 'Umar each fail to answer and instead accuse the questioner of disbelief, which 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas criticises for not even admitting ignorance, before directing the group to 'Ali.

'Ali answers that what is not God's is a partner, what is not with God is injustice, and what God does not know is that the Messiah is God's son — citing 'Do you inform God of what He does not know?' — since the nonexistent has no object of divine knowledge; the questioner then professes Islam and 'Ali's walaya, and 'Ali has al-Hasan and al-Husayn distribute the money to the Muslims.

In a report from Abu al-Jarud via al-Harith al-Awar, a Syrian sent secretly by Mu'awiya brings eleven questions originally posed by Ibn al-Asfar (the Byzantine ruler), who promised to follow and pay tribute to whoever could answer them.

'Ali first detects the stranger's foreignness, grants him safety on the principle that 'when war lays down its burdens there is no harm,' and denounces Mu'awiya and the community that severed his kinship, denied his right and diminished his station.
'Ali defers the questioning to his sons, presenting al-Hasan and al-Husayn as the sons of the Messenger of God and Muhammad (ibn al-Hanafiyya) as his own son, and the Syrian chooses al-Hasan.

Al-Hasan answers all eleven questions — truth and falsehood are four fingers apart (the eye sees truth, the ear hears much falsehood); heaven and earth are separated by the oppressed one's prayer and the reach of sight; east and west by the sun's day-course; the galaxy is the lamps of heaven from which rain descends; the rainbow is God's bow and safeguard from drowning; the moon's darkening is God's erasure of the night's sign per Q 17:12; the first thing to appear on earth was the valley of Dab and the first to stir the palm tree; the polytheists' souls flee to a spring called Salma; the hermaphrodite is identified by emission, menstruation or breasts, else by how the urine strikes a wall; and the ten ascending strengths run stone, iron, fire, water, cloud, wind, angel, Angel of Death, death, and the command of God.

The Syrian testifies that al-Hasan is the son of the Messenger of God and that 'Ali is Muhammad's guardian with more right to the affair than Mu'awiya; and Ibn al-Asfar, on receiving the answers, tells Mu'awiya they come only from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message, not from him, and refuses him even a dirham.

In a further report, 'Ali resolves four of 'Umar's unanswered puzzles: dreams seen while the soul is loosened from the body (per Q 39:42) are true visions of the kingdom while those seen as it returns are Satan's delusion; instinctive love or hatred stems from souls meeting and scenting one another in the air two thousand years before the bodies; and forgetting and recalling are caused by a film over the heart like the film of the moon — after which 'Umar affirms his truthfulness and prays not to outlive him.
